t.2.66.1: But then, not seeing his father there in his father's dwelling, Bharata went to see his mother in his mother's dwelling.
t.2.66.3: As soon as he entered his own house, now bereft of its splendour, the righteous-souled Bharata saw his mother and clasped her auspicious feet.
t.2.66.2: Seeing her son, who had been living abroad, now arrived, Kaikeyī sprang up at once in delight, leaving her golden seat.
t.2.66.4: Having kissed the illustrious Bharata on the head and embraced him, she lifted him onto her lap and began to question him.
t.2.66.5: How many nights has it been now since you left your grandfather's house? Are you not weary from the journey, having come so swiftly by chariot?
t.2.66.7: Thus questioned by Kaikeyī, the lotus-eyed Bharata, son of the king, told his mother everything that was pleasing.
t.2.66.6: Is your grandfather in good health, and Yudhājit, your maternal uncle? And have you returned happily from your stay abroad, my son? You should tell me everything.
t.2.66.8: Today is the seventh night for me since I left my grandfather's house. My mother's father is well, and so is my maternal uncle Yudhājit.
t.2.66.9: The wealth and jewels that the king, scorcher of foes, gave me grew wearisome to carry on the road; therefore I have come on ahead.
t.2.66.10: Hurried along by messengers bearing the king's command, I have come. What I wish to ask, Mother ought to tell me.
t.2.66.11: This gold-adorned couch of yours, meant for lying upon, is empty, and these Ikṣvāku people do not seem to me to be joyful.
t.2.66.12: The king is mostly here, in my mother's residence. I have come here wishing to see him, yet today I do not see him.
t.2.66.13: I shall clasp my father's feet; tell me, who am asking, where he is. Or is he, mother, in the dwelling of the eldest queen, Kausalyā?
t.2.66.14: Kaikeyī, deluded by greed for the kingdom, knowing all while he knew nothing, answered him with terrible, unwelcome news as though it were welcome: "Your father has gone the way that all beings go."
t.2.66.15: Hearing those words, Bharata, pure and of a family devoted to dharma, fell suddenly to the ground, stricken by the force of grief for his father.
t.2.66.16: Then, enveloped by grief and anguished at his father's death, the greatly radiant one lamented, his mind bewildered and distraught.
t.2.66.17: This bed of my father once shone with great splendor; now, bereft of that wise man, it shines no more.
t.2.66.18: Seeing him, godlike and distressed, fallen upon the ground, she raised him up, stricken with grief, and spoke these words.
t.2.66.19: Arise, arise! Why do you lie there, O prince of great renown? For good men such as you, who are honored in the assembly, do not grieve.
t.2.66.20: Having wept for a long time and rolled about upon the ground, he, overwhelmed by many sorrows, spoke these words in reply to his mother.
t.2.66.21: "The king will consecrate Rāma, or perhaps he will perform a sacrifice": with this thought in mind, I joyfully set out on the journey.
t.2.66.23: Mother, of what illness did the king pass away while I had not yet arrived? Fortunate are Rāma and all the others, by whom father was himself given the last rites.
t.2.66.22: For this has turned out otherwise, and my heart is torn apart, I who do not see my father, who was ever devoted to what was dear and good for me.
t.2.66.24: Surely the illustrious great king does not know that I have arrived, for otherwise my father would quickly bend down and kiss me on the head.
t.2.66.25: Where is that hand, so pleasant to the touch, of my father, whose deeds were never wearisome, the hand with which he would again and again wipe me clean when I was covered with dust?
t.2.66.26: Quickly announce my arrival to Rāma, the wise one of tireless deeds, who is my brother, my father and my kinsman, and whose servant I am.
t.2.66.27: For to a noble man who knows dharma, the eldest brother becomes a father. I shall clasp his feet, for he is now my refuge.
t.2.66.28: Noble lady, what did the king, my father, whose valor was truth itself, say? I wish to hear his last good message for me.
t.2.66.29: Thus questioned, Kaikeyī spoke words according to the truth: "Lamenting 'O Rāma!', 'Alas, Sītā!', and 'O Lakṣmaṇa!', the king, that great-souled one, best of those who have attained the goal, has gone to the other world."
t.2.66.30: But your father, seized by the law of time as a great elephant is bound by ropes, uttered these last words.
t.2.66.31: But those men will have their wishes fulfilled who will see Rāma returned together with Sītā, and the mighty-armed Lakṣmaṇa come back again.
t.2.66.32: Hearing that, he was utterly dejected at this second announcement of unwelcome news; and, his face downcast, he questioned his mother again.
t.2.66.33: And where now has he gone, that righteous one who increases Kausalyā's joy, together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa and with Sītā?
t.2.66.34: Thus questioned, his mother began to relate everything just as it had happened, speaking all at once words that were unwelcome, in the belief that they would please him.
t.2.66.35: For that prince, my son, clad in garments of bark, has gone to the great forest of the Daṇḍakas together with Vaidehī, with Lakṣmaṇa following after him.
t.2.66.37: Surely Rāma did not seize the wealth of any brāhmaṇa? Surely he did not harm any innocent man, whether rich or poor?
t.2.66.36: Hearing that, Bharata was alarmed, suspecting some lapse in his brother's conduct, and mindful of the greatness of his own lineage, he began to question her.
t.2.66.39: Then his fickle mother, true to that same womanly nature, began to relate that deed of hers exactly as it had happened.
t.2.66.38: Surely the prince has not desired the wives of other men? Why then was he banished to the Daṇḍaka forest like one who has slain an unborn child?
t.2.66.40: Rāma has not seized any brāhmaṇa's wealth, nor anyone's at all; no innocent man, rich or poor, has ever been harmed by him; and Rāma does not even look upon the wives of others with his eyes.
t.2.66.41: But, my son, as soon as I heard of Rāma's consecration, I asked your father for the kingdom and for the banishment of Rāma.
t.2.66.42: Abiding by his own conduct, your father did just that, and Rāma, together with Saumitri, was sent away along with Sītā.
t.2.66.44: But now, O knower of dharma, let the kingship be taken up by you, for it was for your sake that all this was done by me in this way.
t.2.66.45: Therefore, my son, together with the foremost of the twice-born led by Vasiṣṭha, who are versed in the sacred rules, quickly perform the funeral rites for the king of undaunted spirit, and then have yourself consecrated as ruler of the earth according to the prescribed rite.
t.2.66.43: Not seeing that beloved son, the greatly renowned lord of the earth, wasted by grief for his son, met his death, returning to the five elements.
